verdict.summary: Go packages have a circular dependency - package A imports B and B imports A. The Go specification makes this illegal outright: a package may not import itself, directly or indirectly.

dead_ends.why_fails: Merging removes the cycle by removing the boundary, producing one large package whose internals are all mutually visible. Effective Go's package guidance points the other way - toward small, well-named packages - and the merged package tends to accumulate the next cycle internally instead.

dead_ends.action: Using go:linkname to access unexported symbols
dead_ends.why_fails: //go:linkname deliberately bypasses encapsulation and even type safety, which is why the compiler only honours it in files that import "unsafe". It is also actively being closed off: since Go 1.23 the linker disallows //go:linkname references to standard-library internal symbols that are not themselves marked, so new uses break on upgrade.

workarounds.action: Extract shared types/interfaces into a third package imported by both
workarounds.how: Create a types or models package with the shared definitions

workarounds.action: Use interfaces to break the dependency: depend on abstractions, not implementations
workarounds.how: Package A defines an interface; package B implements it

frequently_confused_with.distinction: 'import cycle not allowed' is a packages error while 'panic' has a different failure mode despite similar symptoms. Check error message details to differentiate.
